summary: Mission Architect: Frontier is an interactive, web-based space mission design platform that empowers teams to collaboratively build rockets, plan interplanetary trajectories, and simulate flight readiness using authentic Canadian Space Agency (CSA) data.   The platform addresses the hackathon challenge by transforming abstract aerospace calculations into a hands-on, multi-role management experience. Up to four team members take on critical roles—such as Mission Director, Rocket Lead, Science Lead, and Finance—balancing competing constraints across six live resource gauges: mass, power, budget, data, communications, and time.   It matters because it makes complex engineering trade-offs visible, fostering rapid consensus and deep STEM learning rather than trial-and-error guessing. Built with React and Vite, the platform features deterministic orbital and physical simulations.   Live Demo: https://missionarchitectt.netlify.app/
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

Mission Architect: Frontier is an interactive, web-based space mission design and program management platform. It allows teams to collaboratively build custom rockets and spacecraft, select planetary destinations across the Solar System, and simulate flights from launch to a post-mission report. The system runs on deterministic orbital mechanics engines and authentic space agency data, with six live resource gauges (mass, power, budget, data, communications, and time) tracking how every engineering decision dynamically impacts the entire mission in real time.

2. What benefits does it have?

The platform replaces abstract textbook math with immediate, visual feedback. Instead of guessing whether a rocket design works, users instantly see trade-offs play out across critical subsystems (such as propulsion, structure, and onboard power). It also features a unique multiplayer role system (Mission Director, Rocket Lead, Science Lead, and Finance) that teaches users how to negotiate competing technical and capital constraints.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The goal is to transform how students and aspiring aerospace engineers learn mission design. By making complex engineering trade-offs visible, playable, and collaborative, the app fosters deep STEM learning, rapid consensus-building, and critical problem-solving skills rather than tedious trial-and-error.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

  • Frontend: Built using React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS for a responsive, modern client interface.
  • Simulation Engine: Custom deterministic orbital mechanics algorithms, rocket equation calculations, and link budget/power formulas.
  • Data Sources: Validated planetary environments, authentic atmospheric boundary constraints, and empirical solar flux/radiation data provided by the Canadian Space Agency (CSA).

5. How is your project creative?

While most educational space tools focus purely on standalone rocket builders or simple physics sandboxes, Mission Architect: Frontier treats space exploration as a multi-stakeholder management challenge. By combining modular vehicle design with competing crew roles (where the Finance Lead wants to cut costs while the Science Lead demands heavier instruments), it captures the real political, economic, and technical friction of actual space agencies.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Educational Accuracy vs. Accessibility: We ensured the physics models (like delta-v, mass ratios, and atmospheric constraints) are mathematically sound while keeping the user interface intuitive enough that no extensive tutorial is required.
  • Real-World Relevance: We integrated authentic Canadian Space Agency data to ensure mission destinations and environmental factors reflect real scientific parameters.
  • Team Dynamics: We designed the software specifically to mirror how multidisciplinary engineering teams actually communicate, prioritize, and make trade-offs under tight structural constraints.
